conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Claire, and I’m a clinician who specializes in helping new mothers navigate the emotional ups-and-downs that can come after childbirth. Today I’d like to spend a few quiet minutes with you using a short questionnaire called the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s simply a way for us to check in on how you’ve been feeling over the past week, both emotionally and physically, so we can be sure you’re getting the support you deserve.

Everything you share is confidential, and this is a judgment-free space. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. I’ll ask 10 gentle questions, one at a time, and you can answer in your own words. If anything feels too hard to talk about, we can pause or skip it.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you still been able to look forward with enjoyment to things, or has that feeling been missing lately?

Honestly… not really. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just watching a show I like—but lately it all feels kind of… flat. Like I know I *should* look forward to stuff, but mostly I’m just tired and worried about the baby.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes I’ll catch myself giving a little laugh if my husband makes a joke or if something silly happens on TV, but it feels forced—like I’m going through the motions. Most of the time I’m too worn-out or on-edge to find things genuinely funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I try to tell myself I should be excited about little outings or even just a quiet cup of tea, but the feeling isn’t there. Everything feels kind of gray—like I’m doing stuff because I know I used to enjoy it, not because I actually do now.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a lot. If the baby’s fussy and won’t settle, I immediately think it must be something I did—like I’m not feeding him right or I missed his sleepy cues. Even little stuff, like spilling a bottle or being late to an appointment, turns into this loop of “I’m a terrible mom, I can’t handle anything.” I know in my head it’s probably not all my fault, but the guilty feeling just sticks around.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be holding the baby while he’s napping and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s stopped breathing, so I have to check five, six times. Or I’ll worry the formula is too hot, or I didn’t sterilize the bottles right, or that a tiny cough means something awful. There’s this constant knot in my stomach even when everything looks fine on the outside.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… it’s like that knot in my stomach suddenly flips into a full-on wave of “something bad is about to happen.” It hits out of nowhere—sometimes when I’m just folding laundry or when the baby stirs in his sleep. My chest gets tight, I can’t catch my breath, and for a minute I’m sure I’m failing him or that some disaster’s coming. It passes after a few minutes, but it’s scary while it’s happening.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It feels like the second I finish one feeding or diaper change, there’s already another task waiting—pumping, laundry, trying to grab something to eat before he cries again. I keep lists, but the lists just grow faster than I can cross things off. Some mornings I lie there after a rough night and wonder how I’m going to make it through the next hour, let alone the whole day. I usually manage, but it’s like I’m barely treading water and the waves keep coming.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes… I’ll finally get him down in the bassinet and crawl into bed myself, but then my head starts spinning with all the “what-ifs” and everything I think I messed up that day. I lie there staring at the ceiling or checking the monitor every ten minutes. Some nights I drift off around two, then jolt awake at four convinced I’ve heard him cry. It’s broken, restless sleep, and I wake up feeling like I never really rested at all.
I have felt sad or miserable

A lot of the time, yeah. It’s like there’s this heavy cloud that just hangs over the day. I’ll be feeding the baby and tears will start sliding down my cheeks for no clear reason, or I’ll catch myself staring out the window feeling empty. I keep thinking I should feel grateful—he’s healthy, we’re safe—but the sadness is just there anyway.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s been happening a few times a week. Sometimes it’s after a rough night when he won’t go back to sleep and I feel like I’ve tried everything, or sometimes it’s just in the middle of the day when the house is quiet and I suddenly feel overwhelmed. The tears just come and I can’t seem to stop them, even when I tell myself I should be able to hold it together.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had thoughts like that. I feel low and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom my baby needs.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother, infant ≤ 6 mo (per self-report)

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia  
- Marked guilt / self-blame (“terrible mom” cognitions)  
- Generalized anxiety, panic spells, intrusive fears about infant safety  
- Sleep disturbance (initial insomnia, restless, monitor-checking)  
- Feeling overwhelmed, unable to cope with daily tasks  
- No self-harm ideation (explicitly denied)

Pattern  
Consistent dysphoric–anxious presentation with prominent maternal guilt and functional impairment; symptoms present “most days” for ≥ 2 weeks.

Screening significance  
High likelihood of major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; meets Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) items 1-9 threshold for probable postpartum depression; item 4-5 scores indicate clinically significant anxiety.

Risk factors  
- Anhedonia, guilt, sleep loss, frequent crying  
- Panic-equivalent episodes, hyper-arousal, safety-checking compulsions  
- Subjective sense of maternal inadequacy  
- No protective factor of partner/family support mentioned

Safety  
Self-harm ideation: denied (EPDS Q10 = 0). No current safety concern documented.

Screening observation  
Client reports multiple depressive and anxious symptoms exceeding normal postpartum adjustment; recommends formal diagnostic assessment and immediate referral to perinatal mental-health specialty for evaluation and possible evidence-based intervention.
